newsitem.title: USA: Dollar and sterling team up to bludgeon mark in US.
newsitem.headline: Dollar and sterling team up to bludgeon mark in US.

text.p: Buoyed by a sharp rise in sterling/mark, the dollar battled back from Thursday's losses and surged to its highest level against the German currency in almost six years during U.S. trade on Friday.

Sterling, which failed to get much mileage out of the Bank of England's decision to raise official British interest rates by a quarter-point on Thursday, soared above 3.0 marks to its highest threshold since October 1990.
The pound was supported by expectations of additional future interest rate rises to rein in soaring consumer demand in Britain.

"The idea of further rate hikes in the UK is making sterling an extremely bullish currency," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York. "And the dollar is getting a lot of help against the mark from the rise in sterling."

The dollar closed at 1.7768/78, then spiked up to a peak of 1.7845 marks in thin trade shortly thereafter -- its highest level since August of 1991. The dollar had opened at 1.7616/19 marks after closing at 1.7513/18 on Thursday.
Friday's mark losses more than erased its solid gains on Thursday, which came in the wake of supportive remarks from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer.
Tietmeyer said that the dollar's correction from early-1995 lows against the mark had come to an end and that mark strength in the run-up to monetary union was important.
"People were leaning the wrong way after Thursday's selloff in the dollar and now they are just selling marks across the board," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co.
"All the mark crosses are getting trampled," he added, citing fund, speculative and corporate interest to sell the German unit.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Friday that the country's total public sector deficit would fall to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, allowing Germany to meet criteria for monetary union and join in the launching of the euro in 1999.
But currency pros remain skeptical of Germany's ability to meet the guidelines and ensure a strong single currency.
Comparatively robust growth in Britain and the United States, and expectations for a a weak euro, have fuelled the active buying of pounds and dollars for marks.
"The US economy just looks too good to be true, especially when you hold it up against what's going on in Germany with its high unemployment," said Strauss.
Reinforcing the positive U.S. economic backdrop on Friday was a Labor Department report which showed that producer prices declined by 0.1 percent in June -- a record sixth consecutive decline.
The benign inflation data pushed bond yields down near 6.5 percent, lending early support to the stock market and dollar, dealers said.
The dollar maintained a firm tone against the yen on Friday, helped by its strength against the mark.
Overnight remarks from former Ministry of Finance vice minister of international affairs Makoto Utsumi provided underpinning.
Utsumi said in an interview with a Japanese daily that financial authorities could intervene to stop the yen's appreciation if the dollar fell below 110 yen.

The dollar ended at 113.98/03 yen, up from 113.69/74 at the open. Elsewhere, the dollar ended higher at 1.4660/70 Swiss francs against 1.4552/62, and flat at Canadian $1.3697/02. The British pound shrank to $1.6895/05 from $1.6980/90.
((-- Noah Barkin, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1673))
